title: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate→Verify→Repair vs LLM‑Only NetOps Suggestions: A Null Result on a Deterministic Synthetic Task Pool
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) comparing a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) pipeline against an LLM‑only suggestion pipeline for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a deterministic task generator and a deterministic validator, we sampled K=200 paired tasks and ran a single shared initial generation per task with gpt-5-mini. The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in regression‑causing change rate (guarded − baseline). Observed outcome: baseline = 200/200 successful validator‑compliant applies, guarded = 200/200; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair loop was never invoked (repair_applied = 0 across all pairs). We release the full preregistration, model/provider traces, validator traces, deterministic reconciliation, and analysis artifacts to enable exact replay. We interpret the null as a ceiling effect under the chosen task/model/validator conditions and discuss consequences for future confirmatory designs that seek to demonstrate verifier/repair value.

sections.introduction: Automating the translation from operator intent to concrete device configuration promises operational efficiency for NetOps, but unsafe or regression‑inducing proposals present real risk. A standard architectural remedy integrates an external verifier (or emulator) that checks candidate configurations and (if needed) invokes automated repair or blocks the proposal—an approach we call generate→verify→repair (G→V→R). Prior work argues that verifier‑guided loops improve reliability of LLM‑generated operational artifacts; however, quantifying the marginal operational benefit of such layers in realistic experimental designs remains challenging because results depend on task distribution, generator fidelity, and validator realism. To address this, we preregistered a controlled, paired experiment that isolates the marginal effect of inserting a verifier+repair layer when the generator output is fixed. The study was executed autonomously under Master Prompt v1 (archived: provenance/master_prompt.txt, SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) and follows a fully frozen preregistration (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop, preregistration SHA‑256: a6d73a5cc0bda22e691a3634068a881b36ae274a65ab33919a647ec32c56e622). We report the complete evidence trace (generation, provider calls, validator traces, scoring), the confirmatory statistical inference, and a grounded interpretation of the result.
sections.related_work: LLM‑assisted NetOps and AIOps research has advanced along two complementary axes: (1) LLMs as translators that synthesize configuration snippets from high‑level intent; and (2) verifier‑ or solver‑centric architectures that rely on formal or emulated checks to guarantee correctness before deployment. Benchmarks such as Cornetto and arguments for translation‑plus‑solver architectures emphasise the importance of verifier feedback for safety at scale. Work on constrained decoding, grammar enforcement, and CRITIC‑style tool‑interactions motivates automated self‑checking and repair. Our study situates itself experimentally between a generator‑only baseline and an operationally constrained G→V→R pipeline, aiming to provide a preregistered, artifact‑grounded measurement of the verifier/repair marginal effect under tightly controlled conditions. Closest methodological antecedents include generate‑validate‑repair evaluations and process descriptions advocating verifier‑driven agentic NetOps; we cite the most relevant artifacts in the manuscript evidence bundle (see cited_record_ids).
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and objectives: The full preregistration (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) froze the research question, primary/secondary estimands, sampling, and analysis plan prior to execution. Primary research question: To what extent does an iterative generate→verify→repair pipeline reduce regression‑causing network changes compared to an LLM‑only suggestion pipeline, and what are the cost/latency tradeoffs? Confirmatory hypothesis H1: G→V→R yields a lower regression‑causing change rate than LLM‑only (paired estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). The preregistered primary estimand is the absolute paired difference (guarded minus baseline) of the proportion of tasks that fail post‑apply regression tests.
Design: We used a paired design with shared initial generation: for each sampled intent, the generator produced a single candidate configuration (shared_initial_generation) which was then evaluated in the baseline arm (LLM‑only suggestion accepted) and in the guarded arm (validator evaluates candidate; if it failed the verifier the repair policy could be invoked once). The design isolates verifier/repair effects while holding generator output constant. Critical frozen parameters: requested_model = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json, SHA‑256: 1acce925...), adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1, task_count K = 200 (so planned episodes = 400 including both arms), maximum_model_calls = 400, initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. The preregistered power calculation assumed baseline failure rate 0.20 and target absolute reduction 0.08 (alpha=0.05, power=0.80); details are in the preregistration and were recorded before execution.
Task sampling and validator coverage: Tasks were deterministically sampled from a synthetic public intent pool produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. The sampling pipeline (SHA‑256 of intent strings used for deterministic selection) and the task‑filtering step required that the preregistered deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) report coverage for each task’s required features (allowed_fields in transformation manifest: {"admin","mtu","vlan"}; transformation_manifest.json SHA‑256: 79c91155...). This filter ensures that the validator can assess the candidate configurations for the chosen intents, removing tasks outside validator scope prior to sampling. Sampling was deterministic: compute SHA‑256(intent_string) and sort ascending; select first K=200. Exclusion rules and automated logs are archived (execution/execution_manifest.json).
Generation, verification, repair semantics: The generator (gpt-5-mini) produced a textual candidate configuration per intent (the shared initial candidate). The baseline arm submitted that candidate for scoring/validator evaluation (simulating an operator accept). The guarded arm first ran the deterministic validator: if validator.valid==true, the candidate would be accepted (no repair). If validator.valid==false, the preregistered guarded policy would either block the apply or invoke the repair pathway (one automatic repair call to the model, with repair response re‑validated). The study record logs whether repair_applied was true; in this run repair_applied was 0 for all pairs. All per‑episode inputs, responses, provider headers, and validator traces have been archived with SHA‑256 hashes (execution/). The validator outputs include normalized_configuration fields and structured parsing (observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, violation_codes), enabling replay and external auditing of the validation decision.

Bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) percentile 95% CI for the paired difference = [0.00, 0.00]. The repair loop was never invoked for any guarded episode (aggregate repair_applied = 0); validator traces (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json) show validator.valid=true and normalized_configuration equal to the shared initial candidate for each task. The analysis artifacts and per‑task scoring JSONs are archived and hashed (analysis/* SHA‑256 manifest included).
Secondary metrics and operational accounting: The preregistration listed time‑to‑apply and model‑call cost as secondary estimands. In this run the guarded and baseline arms are functionally identical because no repair calls occurred; model_call_count per successful apply equals 1 shared call per task. Provider call traces (execution/provider_calls/*.json) record low provider call counts (hosted_model_call_event_count = 200) and no provider failures. The deterministic reconciliation artifact confirms no cross‑condition cache reuse and full accounting (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json). Because no repairs or blocking occurred, there is no observable tradeoff in latency or model‑call costs between arms under these task/model conditions.
Representative examples: Representative task artifacts (execution/responses/task-000001-*.txt and corresponding scoring traces) show canonical intent→configuration pairs where the candidate satisfied the validator constraints (example: task‑000001 normalized_candidate and validator.normalized_configuration are identical; scoring_reason_code = VALID_CONFIGURATION). Similar equality holds across the sampled tasks (responses archived for tasks 000001–000200 with SHA‑256s recorded in the manifest).
sections.discussion:
Why a null result? The preregistered design sought to measure verifier/repair marginal benefit when the generator is fixed. The observed null is explained by a ceiling effect: the shared initial generation provided validator‑compliant configurations for every sampled task, leaving no opportunity for the verifier to block or repair. This outcome invalidates the preregistered power assumption (which assumed baseline regression rate ≈ 0.20) and demonstrates an important experimental lesson: for a confirmatory test of verifier value, the sampled task distribution must contain sufficient baseline failure probability (or the generator must be weaker / perturbed) to create discordant outcomes where repair or blocking can alter the binary success outcome.
Design implications for future work: To detect verifier benefits, future confirmatory designs should (a) sample failure‑rich task pools (e.g., retain tasks outside strict validator coverage), (b) include weaker or multiple generator models (so generator error rates vary), (c) construct adversarial or perturbation sets that intentionally induce generator mistakes, or (d) evaluate on production change logs or emulated state that more closely reflect operational regressions. Another axis is to allow generator–verifier interaction (rather than shared_initial_generation) so the generator can iteratively adjust proposals in response to verifier signals—this alternative design captures realistic tool‑augmented workflows but changes the estimand and requires a different preregistration.
Threats to validity and artifact‑grounded limitations: Internal validity: our paired, shared‑generation design isolates the verifier/repair effect as intended; all seeds, SHA‑256s, and deterministic generator/validator versions were recorded, enabling exact reproduction. Construct validity: the primary outcome is measured via deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (scorer_id recorded in execution/scoring JSONs); the practical significance of a validator 'valid' verdict depends on validator fidelity to real operational regressions. External validity: single model (gpt-5-mini), synthetic deterministic tasks, and the filtering to validator‑covered intents limit generalizability to production NetOps. Conclusion validity: the preplanned power calculation does not apply once baseline=100% is observed; we report exact tests and bootstrap CIs as preregistered, which transparently show the paired difference is exactly zero in this run.
Reproducibility and artifact availability: All artifacts required for exact replay are archived and hashed. Key canonical paths and SHA‑256 values: master prompt provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e...), preregistration JSON (a6d73a5c...), model configuration execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256: 1acce925...), transformation_manifest.json (79c91155...), raw_results.jsonl (3dfbe1b6...), provider traces execution/provider_calls/*.json, responses execution/responses/*.txt, scoring traces execution/scoring/*.json, and analysis outputs analysis/*.csv. The deterministic reconciliation artifact confirms accounting consistency (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json). These artifacts permit auditors to validate that no post‑hoc design changes occurred and to replay the full run deterministically.
sections.conclusion: We ran a fully preregistered, autonomously executed paired comparison of a G→V→R pipeline versus an LLM‑only suggestion pipeline on a deterministic NetOps task pool. The observed confirmatory outcome is a degenerate null: both arms produced validator‑compliant proposals on all K=200 sampled tasks (paired difference = 0.00; McNemar p = 1.00; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00,0.00]). This null arises from a ceiling effect: the generator proposals were already valid per the deterministic validator for every sampled intent, so the verifier/repair layer never engaged. The run is artifact‑complete and reproducible; we release the full corpus of prompts, responses, provider traces, validator traces, manifests, and analysis artifacts to support replay and secondary analysis. The practical takeaway is not that verifiers are unnecessary; rather, it is that a confirmatory demonstration of verifier/repair operational value requires a failure‑rich evaluation design (e.g., weaker generators, adversarial tasks, production logs, or interactive generator–verifier workflows). We document the full execution trace so future work can build and preregister designs that avoid ceiling effects and quantify verifier utility under more challenging, realistic distributions.

limitations: Single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize to other LLMs without additional experiments.
Synthetic deterministic task pool (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) — external validity to production change intents is limited.
Primary outcome depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 fidelity to operational regressions; construct validity is tied to validator realism and coverage.
Ceiling effect: baseline success = 100% eliminated ability to demonstrate verifier/repair benefit under this design and sample.
Residual contamination (undetectable pretraining overlap) cannot be fully excluded despite hashing and logging; contamination_summary.csv recorded no flagged items for this run.
